title: Six partitions, and one of them is doing all the work
intro: The notifications pipeline is hours behind. The team already doubled the consumers from 6 to 12 and it made no difference. The topic 'notifications' has 6 partitions and is keyed by tenant_id. One customer, tenant 7 (a large retailer), ran a big campaign today.

steps.prompt: Check the lag of the consumer group 'notifier' on kafka:9092, partition by partition.
steps.fake_output:

notifier  notifications  1          4398114         4398120         6         notifier-b2
notifier  notifications  2          4402761         4402770         9         notifier-c3

steps.prompt: Partition 3 is 8.7 million messages behind; the rest are fine. Look at what's in it: read 5 messages from partition 3 of 'notifications', printing each message's key.
steps.hint: --partition 3 --property print.key=true shows which keys land there.

steps.prompt: Every message has key 7: one tenant's campaign is all on one partition. Check how many consumers the group has in total.

steps.hint: --members shows how many partitions each consumer was given.

steps.prompt: Six of the twelve consumers have nothing to do: a partition is read by only one consumer in a group. As a stopgap, increase the topic to 24 partitions so new messages spread further.
steps.fake_output:
WARNING: If partitions are increased for a topic that has a key, the partition logic or ordering of the messages will be affected
Adding partitions succeeded!

resolution: Adding consumers couldn't help, for two reasons. A partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group, so 12 consumers on 6 partitions leaves 6 idle. And all of tenant 7's messages share one key, so they all hash to one partition, however many partitions exist. That's a hot partition, the queueing version of the hot key in systemdesign-tutorial-006. Adding partitions is only a stopgap (and Kafka's warning is real: existing keys now map to different partitions, so per-key ordering is broken across the change). The real fix is the key: for notifications, ordering per tenant isn't needed, only per user, so key by user id (or tenant plus user). That spreads a large tenant across every partition while keeping each user's messages in order. Longer term, give very large tenants their own topic or apply per-tenant rate limits, so one customer's campaign can't delay everyone else's password-reset emails.
